metadata.title: A new macroeconomic measure of human capital exploiting PISA and PIAAC: Linking education policies to productivity (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD working paper constructs macroeconomic human-capital measures by linking internationally comparable test-score information from PISA (student skills at age 15) and PIAAC (adult skills for working-age cohorts), then uses these constructed series in productivity regressions. The analysis is conducted at the country and cohort level (e.g., cohort-weighted averages of adult and student test scores, and country-level mean years of schooling), rather than estimating student-level models from microdata. As a result, the paper does not report the application of complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) typical of ILSA microdata analyses. For analysts wishing to reproduce or extend the work with microdata, appropriate PISA/PIAAC sampling weights and replicate weights should be applied when estimating student/adult test-score summaries, but this paper’s published methodology focuses on macro aggregation and time-series/cross-sectional econometric estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not estimate student-level cognitive outcomes using ILSA Plausible Values (PV) or report PV-based model fitting; instead, it constructs cohort- and country-level measures from PISA and PIAAC test-score summaries and then uses these in macroeconomic productivity regressions. Missing-data handling is therefore not documented in the sense of PV imputation/deletion at the microdata level, because the paper’s core contribution is the macro measure construction and econometric testing rather than PV-based ML on microdata. This should be treated as a reporting gap for PV/missing-data transparency if one attempts to replicate the constructed score series from microdata.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper constructs cohort-matched student and adult test-score series by linking PIAAC adult test scores (literacy, numeracy, problem solving) to PISA student test scores for the corresponding cohorts aged 15 at the time of testing, using lagging and (where needed) adjustments of 1–2 years. It then extends PISA time series backwards using World Bank Global Dataset on Education Quality (Altinok et al., 2018) and applies availability constraints: (i) the PIAAC–PISA matching analysis uses the set of countries for which both PIAAC and extended PISA cohort scores are available (35 countries for the correlation/matching exercise); (ii) the full working-age stock measure (16–65) is computed for a limited number of countries with sufficiently long student-score series (reported as 15 OECD countries for the comprehensive 16–65 measure); and (iii) a shorter stock measure (16–39) is computed for a larger set of countries (54 countries in the last available year). For productivity regressions, the analytic samples are further restricted to the countries with the constructed human-capital measure and the required productivity-policy covariates (e.g., OECD-only availability for some regulation/R&D variables, with substitutions for non-OECD).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops a new macroeconomic “stock of human capital” that combines the quantity of education (mean years of schooling) with the quality of education (student test scores from PISA linked to adult skills from PIAAC). The key methodological step is estimating the relative elasticities of adult test scores with respect to cohort-matched student test scores and mean years of schooling, and then using these estimated weights to cumulate quality and quantity across cohorts in the working-age population. The resulting human-capital measure is used in OECD QASR-style productivity regressions, including both cross-country time-series panel models for OECD countries and purely cross-sectional models for a broader set of countries. The paper reports that the new measure is robustly positively associated with multi-factor productivity and that simulated, sustained improvements in student test scores yield larger long-run productivity gains than comparable increases in mean years of schooling, though with very long lags (nearly five decades) for student-skill improvements to fully affect the working-age stock. The analysis is macro-aggregated and does not involve student-level ML or PV-based estimation, so survey-weight and PV-handling transparency is not applicable in the usual ILSA microdata sense.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a macroeconomic measurement and econometric framework paper rather than an empirical ML/predictive study on ILSA microdata. It does not train machine-learning models, does not report PV-based predictive performance metrics, and does not provide student-level sample sizes or per-country student counts for an analytic dataset. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques, PV handling, and missing-data handling at the micro/PV level are either not applicable or not reported, while the core contribution is the construction of a new human-capital stock measure and its macroeconomic associations.
